reference_answer: The factory pattern separates work into three object-building steps: Index.from_variables constructs the index; Coordinates.from_xindex immediately calls index.create_variables(), builds a name-to-index mapping, and constructs Coordinates; assign_coords makes a shallow copy of the caller and updates its Coordinates, whose update path merges coordinate/index mappings before returning a new object. This adds Python object construction, mapping creation/copying, and coordinate merge bookkeeping as the number of variables grows. Dataset.set_xindex is a more integrated path: it constructs the index, calls create_variables with existing coordinate variables, updates copied/rebuilt variable and index mappings, and replaces the dataset once. However, at this commit set_xindex deliberately rejects indexes that create extra coordinate variables and tells callers to use the factory pattern. The excerpts establish structural overhead and an optimization opportunity, but they do not benchmark throughput, prove data-buffer copying, or justify a numeric speedup such as 2–3x.
required_facts: Trace the factory pattern through index creation, from_xindex create_variables/mapping construction, and assign_coords shallow-copy plus coordinate merge/update.
Compare with set_xindex as an integrated mapping-update path while noting it rejects extra variables and recommends the factory pattern for that case.
State the evidence boundary: the source supports extra object/mapping/merge work, but not a measured throughput ratio or universal data copying claim.

reference_provenance.correction: Removes unsupported 2-3x and repeated-data-materialization claims; source establishes control-flow overhead but contains no performance measurement.
